claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Lys257 stacks onto U4532.
claims.source: Lys257 also stacks onto U4532, and this stacking interaction might influence the movement of the critical PTC base U4531 (U2585 in E. coli) (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The stacking interaction between Lys257 and U4532 might influence the movement of the critical PTC base U4531.
claims.source: Lys257 also stacks onto U4532, and this stacking interaction might influence the movement of the critical PTC base U4531 (U2585 in E. coli) (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claims.claim: Five of the eight residues that constitute the turn engage in contacts with the tunnel.
claims.source: Taken together, five of the eight residues that constitute the turn engage in contacts with the tunnel.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of structural observations.

claims.claim: Tyr241 of XBP1u stacks with C2794 of 28S rRNA.
claims.source: In the distal part of the tunnel, Tyr241 of XBP1u stacks with C2794 of 28S rRNA (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Arg71 and Ser87 of uL4, as well as Arg128 of uL22 make contacts mostly with the backbone of the nascent chain.
claims.source: Three of the remaining interactions of the nascent chain in the distal tunnel region are mediated by the constriction proteins uL4 and uL22, respectively. Here, Arg71 and Ser87 of uL4, as well as Arg128 of uL22 make contacts mostly with the backbone of the nascent chain (Figure 3J - L).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3J-L.

claims.claim: U4531 (U2585 in E. coli) is in its canonical upward conformation in the XBP1u-stalled RNC.
claims.source: In contrast to some bacterial APs, we observed U4531 (U2585) in the XBP1u-stalled RNC in its canonical upward conformation.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: U4531 interacts with the side chain of Met260 but appears not to be hindered from switching downwards upon A-site accommodation.
claims.source: Although it interacts with the side chain of Met260 (Figure 3C), it appears that this base would not be hindered to switch downwards upon A-site accommodation to adopt the induced conformation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: C4398 (C2452) is in the closed conformation in the XBP1u-stalled RNC.
claims.source: However, another nucleotide, C4398 (C2452), is in the closed conformation (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), a position that under normal conditions is observed only after A-site accommodation, as in the reconstruction of the yeast 80S ribosome with A-, P-site tRNA and eIF5a (PDB 5GAK) (Schmidt et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: C4398 is stabilized in the closed conformation by Leu259.
claims.source: C4398 (C2452) is stabilized in the closed conformation by Leu259, which, in contrast to Met260, cannot be mutated to alanine without almost entirely loosing stalling activity (see below).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and supported by mutagenesis data.

claims.claim: C4398 (C2452) has been implicated in A-site tRNA accommodation and peptidyl transferase activity.
claims.source: Notably, this base has been implicated in A-site tRNA accommodation and peptidyl transferase activity.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of this base.

claims.claim: The premature positioning of C4398 in the closed conformation provides a mechanistic explanation for PTC inactivation by inhibition of A-site tRNA accommodation.
claims.source: Therefore, the premature positioning of C4398 (C2452) in the closed conformation due to its interaction with Leu259 in an unusual conformation provides a mechanistic explanation for PTC inactivation by inhibition of A-site tRNA accommodation: Leu259 would simply clash with the incoming Asn261 tRNA (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Leu259 would clash with the incoming Asn261 tRNA.
claims.source: Therefore, the premature positioning of C4398 (C2452) in the closed conformation due to its interaction with Leu259 in an unusual conformation provides a mechanistic explanation for PTC inactivation by inhibition of A-site tRNA accommodation: Leu259 would simply clash with the incoming Asn261 tRNA (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Inhibition or delay of tRNA accommodation into the A-site appears to be the main mechanism for translational pausing by the XBP1u AP.
claims.source: Therefore, inhibition or delay of tRNA accommodation into the A-site appears to be the main mechanism for translational pausing by the XBP1u AP.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claims.claim: No stable class of ribosomes carrying a canonical A-site tRNA was found in the population of stalled RNCs.
claims.source: This idea is further supported by the observation that we do not find a stable class of ribosomes in our population of stalled RNCs that carry a canonical A-site tRNA.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from cryo-EM data processing.

claims.claim: A substantial fraction of the RNCs is in the rotated state.
claims.source: Moreover, it can be easily imagined how pulling force applied to the nascent chain can rectify the only mildly perturbed geometry of the PTC and thereby alleviate stalling. Since we detect a substantial fraction of the RNCs in the rotated state (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) we cannot exclude that the XBP1u structure may also perturb translocation as well as preventing rapid A-site tRNA accommodation.
claims.evidence: This is observed in cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: No perturbation of the P-tRNA 3'-CCA end pairing with the P-loop in 28S rRNA was observed.
claims.source: However, we do not observe any perturbation of the P-tRNA 3'-CCA end pairing with the P-loop in 28S rRNA, as was seen in other cases (Li et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure, contrasted with cited cases.

claims.claim: The entire XBP1u AP contributes to pausing by interacting with the tunnel to form a unique turn structure.
claims.source: Taken together, the entire XBP1u AP contributes to pausing by interacting with the tunnel to form a unique turn structure and, facilitated by this structure, stabilizing the PTC in a conformation that disfavors A-site accommodation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on structural observations.

claims.claim: The XBP1u AP stabilizes the PTC in a conformation that disfavors A-site accommodation.
claims.source: Taken together, the entire XBP1u AP contributes to pausing by interacting with the tunnel to form a unique turn structure and, facilitated by this structure, stabilizing the PTC in a conformation that disfavors A-site accommodation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on structural observations.

claims.claim: The final reconstruction of XBP1u-RNC-SRP had an average resolution of 3.7 Å.
claims.source: The final reconstruction had an average resolution of 3.7 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and the SRP itself was resolved between 5–10 Å (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM structure determination.

claims.claim: SRP was resolved between 5–10 Å in the XBP1u-RNC-SRP structure.
claims.source: The final reconstruction had an average resolution of 3.7 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and the SRP itself was resolved between 5–10 Å (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from cryo-EM structure determination.

claims.claim: A clear rod-like density resembling a signal sequence was observed in the hydrophobic groove of the SRP54 M-domain.
claims.source: Analysis of the hydrophobic groove of the SRP54 M-domain, which is known to mediate the recognition and binding of canonical signal sequences, revealed a clear rod-like density resembling that of a signal sequence (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The rod-like density in the SRP54 M-domain likely represents the SRP-bound HR2 domain.
claims.source: Since the only sufficiently hydrophobic peptide stretch available is HR2 of XBP1u, it is highly likely that this density indeed represents the SRP-bound HR2 domain, bound in a conformation indistinguishable from that of normal SRP-bound signal sequences.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations and the known composition of the complex.

claims.claim: The exposed HR2 domain on the paused XBP1u-RNC forms a helical structure upon successful SRP recruitment.
claims.source: Hence, we conclude that the exposed HR2 domain on the paused XBP1u-RNC forms a helical structure upon successful SRP recruitment, which makes a canonical interaction with the M-domain of SRP54.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural observations.

claims.claim: The conformation of the AP is identical in the presence of SRP to that of the RNC alone.
claims.source: Notably, the nascent chain density was sufficiently well resolved within the tunnel of the XBP1u-RNC-SRP complex to allow for molecular model building. At the given resolution, the conformation of the AP is identical in the presence of SRP to that of the RNC alone.
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing the two cryo-EM structures.

claims.claim: SRP binding to paused XBP1u-RNCs does not lead to perturbation of the nascent chain within the tunnel.
claims.source: The finding that SRP binding to paused XBP1u-RNCs does not lead to perturbation of the nascent chain within the tunnel strongly suggests that this state maintains the RNC in the paused state.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: The XBP1u-RNC-Sec61 complex represents the idle state with the lateral gate of the translocon in a closed conformation.
claims.source: When comparing with known structures of Sec61, we found that our structure represented the idle state with the lateral gate of the translocon, mainly formed by TM2 and TM7, in a closed conformation (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing the cryo-EM structure with known Sec61 structures, shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: No additional density for the HR2 domain of XBP1u was identified on or near the Sec61 complex.
claims.source: We could not identify any additional density for the HR2 domain of XBP1u on or near the Sec61 complex, indicating a rather weak or transient interaction.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: Less than 10% of XBP1u becomes integrated into the ER membrane.
claims.source: Considering the low hydrophobicity of the HR2 domain and previous biochemical evidence that less than 10% of XBP1u becomes integrated into the ER membrane (Plumb et al., 2015), our data are in full agreement with the idea that HR2 can interact with, but cannot productively engage and gate, the Sec61 translocon.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Plumb et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The structure of the XBP1u nascent chain in the XBP1u-RNC-Sec61-complex is indistinguishable from the structures observed in the XBP1u-RNC and the XBP1u-RNC-SRP complexes.
claims.source: The structure of the XBP1u nascent chain in the XBP1u-RNC-Sec61-complex is indistinguishable from the structures observed in the XBP1u-RNC and the XBP1u-RNC-SRP complexes, with RMSDs between the structures in the range of about 1 Å (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is determined by structural comparison shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: There is no change in the pausing efficiency during or after successful targeting to the ER membrane.
claims.source: This finding strongly suggests that there is no change in the pausing efficiency during or after successful targeting to the ER membrane, and XBP1u is therefore unlikely to act as a force-sensitive translational switch in the UPR.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claims.claim: XBP1u is unlikely to act as a force-sensitive translational switch in the UPR.
claims.source: This finding strongly suggests that there is no change in the pausing efficiency during or after successful targeting to the ER membrane, and XBP1u is therefore unlikely to act as a force-sensitive translational switch in the UPR.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claims.claim: The long linker length of 52 amino acids between the HR2 domain and the arrest peptide prevents potential force transmission.
claims.source: Probably the long linker length of 52 amino acids between the HR2 domain and the arrest peptide prevents any potential force applied to HR2 upon interaction with SRP or Sec61 to be transmitted to the XBP1u AP.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural considerations.

claims.claim: Mutations P254→[V,I,C], Q253→N, and C247→[N, K] have fFL values < 0.5.
claims.source: Particularly strong reductions in fFL were seen for mutations P254→[V,I,C], Q253→N, and C247→[N, K], that all have fFL values < 0.5.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from mutagenesis experiments.

claims.claim: Eight residues in the wildtype XBP1u AP are optimal for efficient translational arrest under a strong pulling force.
claims.source: Eight residues in the wildtype XBP1u AP are optimal for efficient translational arrest under a strong pulling force (i.e., all mutations lead to an increase in fFL): Y241, P244, W249 to H252, W256, and P258.
claims.evidence: This is a result from saturation mutagenesis experiments.

claims.claim: Five of the eight turn residues are optimal for translational arrest.
claims.source: Not surprisingly, the turn region W249-W256 stands out: five of the eight turn residues are optimal for translational arrest.
claims.evidence: This is a result from saturation mutagenesis experiments.

claims.claim: P244 makes a hydrogen bond to R71 in uL4.
claims.source: P244 makes a hydrogen bond to R71 in uL4 (Figure 3J) that may be weakened if the highly constrained backbone geometry of P244 is not maintained, and Y241 makes an apparently important stacking interaction with C2794 (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3J.

claims.claim: 55 mutations in Q242, P243, F245, L246, C247, Q248, Q253, P254, S255, K257, L259, and M260 lead to reduced fFL values.
claims.source: In contrast, some residues in the wildtype AP are clearly sub-optimal in terms of arrest potency, and we find no less than 55 mutations in Q242, P243, F245, L246, C247, Q248, Q253, P254, S255, K257, L259, and M260 that lead to reduced fFL values (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from saturation mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Mutation of C247 to charged or polar residues increases the stalling strength.
claims.source: Mutation of C247 to charged or polar residues increases the stalling strength. These residues presumably interact with the ribosomal tunnel by forming hydrogen bonds or salt-bridges with the phosphate backbone of rRNA, but the precise interactions cannot be easily predicted from the structure.
claims.evidence: This is a result from mutagenesis experiments, with inference about mechanism.

claims.claim: Mutating Q253 to Asn leads to strong increase in the translational arrest.
claims.source: Q253 is part of the turn, and mutating it to Asn leads to strong increase in the translational arrest.
claims.evidence: This is a result from mutagenesis experiments.

claims.claim: Nine mutations in P254 increase the stalling strength.
claims.source: Nine mutations in the neighboring residue P254 also increase the stalling strength, albeit to varying levels.
claims.evidence: This is a result from mutagenesis experiments.

claims.claim: The XBP1u turn is similar to a β-turn, but does not satisfy all the geometrical parameters.
claims.source: The XBP1u turn is similar to a β-turn, but does not satisfy all the geometrical parameters and therefore is probably less stable than a canonical β-turn.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: Proline is not favored in β-turns.
claims.source: Proline is not favored in β-turns, and its presence in the turn of the XBP1u nascent chain might be a result of evolution favoring weaker translational pausing instead of a highly efficient arrest.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about β-turn structure and inference about evolutionary selection.

claims.claim: The mutagenesis data is entirely consistent with the evolutionary conservation of the XBP1u AP.
claims.source: The mutagenesis data is entirely consistent with the evolutionary conservation of the XBP1u AP, as seen in the Logo plot in Figure 6E.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing mutagenesis data with evolutionary conservation shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: None of the sequence variants in the natural XBP1u APs lead to a strong decrease in fFL.
claims.source: None of the sequence variants in the natural XBP1u APs lead to a strong decrease in fFL according to Figure 6C (the maximal decrease is from fFL = 0.89 to fFL = 0.52 for C247H) and, to the extent that they have been tested, none of the sequence variants in the natural APs (except S255) lead to a strong increase in fFL according to Figure 6D (the maximal increase is from fFL = 0.46 to fFL = 0.61 for P244A and R251P).
claims.evidence: This is a result from comparing natural variants with mutagenesis data in Figure 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: S255 is completely conserved despite the fact that the S255A mutant has much stronger arrest potency.
claims.source: It is especially noteworthy that S255 is completely conserved despite the fact that the S255A mutant has much stronger arrest potency (Figure 6D), and that the strong Q253N mutation has not been seen so far in a natural sequence.
claims.evidence: This is observed from evolutionary conservation data and mutagenesis results in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The XBP1u AP is under selective pressure to maintain a rather weak translational arrest efficiency.
claims.source: We conclude that, although the turn region in the XBP1u AP includes many residues that are optimal for translational pausing, the XBP1u AP is under selective pressure to maintain a rather weak translational arrest efficiency.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on mutagenesis and evolutionary conservation data.

claims.claim: The XBP1u AP carrying mutations S255A and P254C reduces fFL values throughout the force profile while the shape of the profile persists.
claims.source: To evaluate the possible use of mutant XBP1u APs in such contexts, we re-measured the force profile in Figure 6B using a strong XBP1u AP carrying the mutations S255→A and P254→C (blue curve in Figure 6B; see Supplementary file 2 for sequences). fFL values are reduced throughout, while the shape of the profile persists.
claims.evidence: This is a result from force profile measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The P254C mutation reduces the AP's sensitivity to both high and low pulling forces.
claims.source: The P254C mutation thus reduces the APs sensitivity to both high and low pulling forces (i.e., both at the peak around L = 40–45 residues and at L ≥ 55 residues), suggesting that results obtained under high pulling forces (e.g., Figure 6C and D) can be extrapolated to the low-force situation that presumably applies when the XBP1u AP performs its normal function in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on force profile data.

claims.claim: No crosslinked product is apparent when a gel is run under non-reducing conditions for the P254C mutant.
claims.source: Because the mutant AP has a Cys residue in position 254, we considered that the enhanced arrest potency may be due to the formation of a disulfide bond with a ribosomal protein, or within the nascent chain itself. However, no crosslinked product is apparent when a gel is run under non-reducing conditions, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, and fFL is even slightly reduced (as expected from Figure 6C) when the other Cys residue in the AP (C247) is mutated to Ser, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The early peak at L ≈ 30 residues seen for the SecM AP in E. coli is not clearly seen in the mammalian force profiles.
claims.source: Interestingly, the early peak at L ≈ 30 residues seen for the same H-segment constructs expressed in E. coli with the SecM AP (Ismail et al., 2012) (gray curve, Figure 6B) is not clearly seen in the mammalian force profiles, suggesting that the H segment interacts differently with the Sec61 and SecYEG translocons at early stages of membrane insertion.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing force profiles, with citation to Ismail et al., 2012.

claims.claim: XBP1u functions in a unique manner compared to previously described arrest peptides.
claims.source: As with previously described APs, XBP1u apparently functions in a unique manner.
claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: PTC bases U4531 (U2585), U4452 (U2506) and A4548 (A2602) are known to be critical in translation elongation and termination.
claims.source: PTC bases which are known to be critical in translation elongation and termination are U4531 (U2585), U4452 (U2506) and A4548 (A2602) and, consequently, these bases are often perturbed by APs to inactivate ribosomes (Wilson et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2016.

claims.claim: U4531 (U2585) is the most often distorted base by arrest peptides.
claims.source: Among these, the most often distorted base is U4531 (U2585) which needs to be precisely positioned for both peptide bond formation and nascent chain release (Schmeing et al., 2005; Youngman et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmeing et al., 2005; Youngman et al., 2004.

claims.claim: XBP1u functions similarly to some arrest peptides by preventing A-site tRNA accommodation, but in a unique manner.
claims.source: Therefore, compared to previously described APs, XBP1u functions similarly to some of them by preventing A-site tRNA accommodation (Arenz et al., 2014; Sohmen et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017), however, in a unique manner (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural comparison, with citations to Arenz et al., 2014; Sohmen et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The saturation mutagenesis experiments demonstrate that the XBP1u AP has not evolved to maximize its resistance to pulling forces on the nascent chain.
claims.source: It was known before that mutation of critical residues involved in the described XBP1u mechanism resulted in loss of stalling activity, however, one mutation (S255A) turned out to be enhancing. Notably, our saturation mutagenesis experiments demonstrate that the XBP1u AP has not evolved to maximize its resistance to pulling forces on the nascent chain, and that many more enhancing mutations exist.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on mutagenesis data.

claims.claim: P254 plays a critical role in arrest potency, since nine other residues in this position can all impart stronger arrest potency on the AP.
claims.source: P254 plays a critical role in this regard, since nine other residues in this position can all impart stronger arrest potency on the AP.

results.result: The authors determined a 3 Å cryo-EM structure of the stalled human XBP1u arrest peptide (using the S255A mutant) in complex with the ribosome. The structure reveals that the XBP1u AP forms a unique turn comprised of eight residues (W249-W256) in the ribosomal exit tunnel, located only four residues away from the peptidyl transferase center (PTC), with ribosomes paused at Met260 in the P-site.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C40-C54, and C58 collectively provide strong structural evidence for the 3 Å resolution structure showing the unique turn formation. The cryo-EM data processing yielded 531,952 particles with ~60% programmed ribosomes, and the structure was resolved to 3.0 Å for the post state and 3.1 Å for the rotated state. The structural characterization of the turn and its proximity to the PTC is well-documented with specific residue assignments and measurements.

results.result: The XBP1u AP establishes extensive molecular interactions with the ribosomal tunnel. The turn is framed by two tryptophan residues (W249 and W256), protrudes into a hydrophobic crevice causing displacement of base G3904, and five of the eight turn residues engage in specific contacts with tunnel components including salt bridges, hydrogen bonds, and stacking interactions with rRNA bases and ribosomal proteins uL4 and uL22.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C73 describe detailed molecular interactions observed in the cryo-EM structure at 3.0-3.5 Å resolution. The interactions are specific and well-characterized, including the salt bridge between Arg251 and A4388, hydrogen bonds from Gly250 and Gln253 to rRNA bases, and stacking interactions. These structural observations are supported by the high-resolution density maps shown in the figures.

results.result: The XBP1u AP causes translational pausing by a unique mechanism involving premature positioning of base C4398 (C2452) in the closed conformation, stabilized by Leu259. This positioning would cause Leu259 to clash with incoming A-site tRNA, thereby inhibiting or delaying A-site tRNA accommodation rather than perturbing the canonical PTC base U4531 (U2585).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C86 provide a mechanistic explanation supported by structural observations and modeling. The structure shows C4398 in the closed conformation before A-site accommodation, which is unusual. The modeling demonstrates that Leu259 would clash with incoming Asn261 tRNA (C80). The absence of stable A-site tRNA-containing ribosomes in the dataset (C82) and the substantial fraction in rotated state (C83) support this mechanism. The structural evidence is consistent and well-reasoned.

results.result: The XBP1u AP adopts a unique structural conformation compared to other characterized arrest peptides. While the distal parts of the tunnel show similarity to other nascent chains, the turn structure is unique and located in a region where other APs adopt α-helical secondary structure. XBP1u functions similarly to some APs by preventing A-site tRNA accommodation but through a distinct mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C60, C119, and C122 are supported by structural comparisons shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and discussed in the text. The comparisons with Sec61b, CMV, MifM, and VemP structures demonstrate both similarities in the distal tunnel region and the uniqueness of the turn structure. The conclusion that XBP1u functions uniquely is well-supported by the structural data and mechanistic analysis.

results.result: During ribosomal pausing, the HR2 domain of XBP1u is recognized by SRP in a canonical manner. The cryo-EM structure of XBP1u-RNC-SRP at 3.7 Å resolution shows clear rod-like density in the SRP54 M-domain hydrophobic groove, likely representing HR2 in a helical conformation. Importantly, SRP binding does not alter the conformation of the arrest peptide within the ribosomal tunnel.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C87-C93 are supported by the cryo-EM structure of the XBP1u-RNC-SRP complex. The 3.7 Å resolution structure shows clear density for SRP and the rod-like density in the M-domain (C89, Figure 5B). The inference that this represents HR2 (C90) is reasonable given it's the only sufficiently hydrophobic region available. The structural comparison showing identical AP conformation with and without SRP (C92) is well-documented with RMSD ~1 Å (C97).

results.result: HR2 of XBP1u fails to efficiently gate the Sec61 translocon. The cryo-EM structure shows Sec61 in the idle state with closed lateral gate, no additional density for HR2 on Sec61, and the nascent chain conformation remains unaltered (RMSD ~1 Å) across all three states (RNC alone, RNC-SRP, RNC-Sec61). This indicates XBP1u is unlikely to act as a force-sensitive translational switch, possibly due to the long 52 amino acid linker between HR2 and the arrest peptide.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C94-C100, C128-C129 are well-supported by structural data from three different complexes. The Sec61 structure shows the idle state with closed lateral gate (C94), absence of HR2 density (C95), and identical AP conformation across all states with RMSD ~1 Å (C97). The conclusion about force-insensitivity (C98-C99) is a reasonable inference from these observations. The linker length argument (C100, C132) is supported by force profile data (C131) showing maximal force at 43 residues vs. 52 residues in XBP1u.

results.result: Saturation mutagenesis of the XBP1u AP revealed that only 8 out of 20 mutagenized positions are optimal for translational arrest, while 55 different mutations in 12 positions increase arrest potency. Key mutations include P254→[V,I,C], Q253→N, and C247→[N,K] with fFL < 0.5. The mutagenesis data is consistent with evolutionary conservation, demonstrating that the wildtype XBP1u AP is under selective pressure to maintain intermediate (rather than maximal) translational arrest efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9, C101-C108, C111-C114, C123-C125 are strongly supported by comprehensive saturation mutagenesis data presented in Figure 6C and 6D. The quantitative fFL measurements show clear patterns of optimal and sub-optimal positions. The evolutionary conservation analysis (C111, Figure 6E) supports the conclusion that the wildtype sequence maintains intermediate arrest strength. The finding that S255 is completely conserved despite S255A having stronger arrest (C113) particularly supports the selective pressure argument (C114).

results.result: Stronger variants of the XBP1u AP (S255A/P254C double mutant) can be used as force sensors. The double mutant reduces fFL values throughout the force profile while maintaining the profile shape, and the P254C mutation reduces sensitivity to both high and low pulling forces. The enhanced arrest is not due to disulfide bond formation, as demonstrated by non-reducing gel analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 and C126 are supported by force profile measurements (Figure 6B) and control experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A). The force profile data clearly shows reduced fFL throughout while maintaining shape (C115). The absence of crosslinked products under non-reducing conditions (C117) rules out disulfide-mediated enhancement. The conclusion about utility as force sensors (C126) is a reasonable inference from the data, though actual application would require further validation.

results.result: The authors propose a model for XBP1u function in the UPR: the AP pauses ribosomes sufficiently for HR2 to recruit SRP, enabling ER targeting and efficient IRE1α-mediated splicing. Neither SRP nor Sec61 release the stall, which likely resolves autonomously (more probable than Pelota/Hbs1-mediated recycling given the weak wildtype AP). The pausing may have evolved as a precise timer for co-translational mRNA localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C140 represent a proposed model and mechanistic interpretation. While C133-C135 are well-supported by the structural data showing unaltered AP conformation across states, claims C136-C140 are speculative scenarios about the fate of paused complexes and evolutionary purpose. The preference for autonomous resolution (C138) is reasoned but not directly tested. The 'timer' hypothesis (C140) is plausible but remains speculative. These represent reasonable interpretations but lack direct experimental validation.

results.result: The early peak at L ≈ 30 residues seen for SecM AP in E. coli is not clearly observed in mammalian force profiles with XBP1u AP, suggesting differential interactions of the H segment with Sec61 versus SecYEG translocons at early membrane insertion stages.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 is supported by comparison of force profiles in Figure 6B, showing the mammalian profiles (red and blue curves) lack the early peak present in the E. coli SecM profile (gray curve). This is a valid comparative observation, though the mechanistic interpretation about differential translocon interactions is inferential.

results.result: The XBP1u turn is similar to a β-turn but does not satisfy all geometrical parameters and is probably less stable than a canonical β-turn. The presence of proline (not favored in β-turns) might reflect evolution favoring weaker translational pausing.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 represent structural analysis and evolutionary inference. The observation that the turn resembles but doesn't match a canonical β-turn (C109) is based on structural analysis. The inference about proline disfavoring β-turns and evolutionary selection for weaker pausing (C110) is reasonable given the mutagenesis data showing many mutations strengthen arrest, but remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Force profile analysis shows maximal accumulation of full-length product at a linker length of 43 amino acids, while in stalled XBP1u, HR2 is approximately 52 amino acids distant from the PTC.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132 are supported by force profile measurements (Figure 6B) and structural/sequence analysis. The 43 amino acid optimal linker length is directly measured from the force profile, and the 52 amino acid distance in XBP1u is determined from the structure and sequence. These are factual observations used to support the force-insensitivity argument.

results.result: Background and context claims about arrest peptides, UPR pathway, XBP1u structure and function, and ribosomal mechanisms based on prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C39, C63-C64, C120-C121 represent established knowledge from the literature, supported by appropriate citations. These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings from this work. The citations appear appropriate and the background information is accurately represented.
